blocks.text: **The problem.** Rotate an n × n matrix **90 degrees clockwise**, modifying it **in place** — you may not allocate another matrix.

blocks.alt: Rotating [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]] clockwise gives [[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]. Colours follow each original row: the first row (yellow) becomes the last column.

blocks.text: Example
Understanding the problem
Study the colours and the rule appears: the first **row** becomes the last **column**, the second row becomes the middle column, and so on. As a formula, the value at `(r, c)` moves to:

The hard part is the words **in place**. Moving one value to its new home overwrites whatever was there, and that value must move somewhere too — which overwrites another. Values travel in cycles of four.
Brute force: use a second matrix

Placing each value directly is easy with a second matrix — but that's **O(n²) extra space**, which the problem forbids. Chasing the four-element cycles in place works, but the index arithmetic is painful to get right under pressure.
The key insight: two easy moves make one hard move
A 90° clockwise rotation is the same as a **transpose** (mirror across the main diagonal) followed by **reversing every row**. Both of those are simple, and both can be done in place:

blocks.alt: Three grids: the start [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]; after transposing, [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]]; after reversing each row, [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].
blocks.caption: After the transpose, each original row sits in a column — just upside down. Reversing the rows flips it the right way up.

blocks.text: Why the inner loop starts at r + 1

Transposing swaps `(r, c)` with `(c, r)`. If the inner loop started at 0, every pair would be visited **twice** — once as `(r, c)` and once as `(c, r)` — and the second swap would undo the first, leaving the matrix unchanged.
Starting at `c = r + 1` visits only the cells **above** the diagonal, so each pair is swapped exactly once. The diagonal itself is skipped, because `(r, r)` would swap with itself.
Dry run it yourself
First watch the mirror swaps above the diagonal, then each row reversing. Try a 4 × 4 matrix too.
Code

blocks.code:
def rotate(matrix):
    n = len(matrix)
    for r in range(n):                      # 1. transpose
        for c in range(r + 1, n):
            matrix[r][c], matrix[c][r] = matrix[c][r], matrix[r][c]
    for row in matrix:                      # 2. reverse each row
        row.reverse()

blocks.text: Complexity

blocks.alt: Second matrix: O(n²) time and O(n²) space. Transpose then reverse: O(n²) time and O(1) space.

blocks.text: Every value is touched a constant number of times: **O(n²) time, O(1) extra space**.
Edge cases to test

items: **4 × 4** — an even size, where there is no single middle value.

blocks.text: Counter-clockwise, and beyond

To rotate **counter-clockwise**, reverse each row **first**, then transpose — the same two moves in the opposite order. Rotating by 180° is simply reversing each row and then reversing the order of the rows.

The lesson generalises far beyond matrices: a transformation that is awkward to do directly is often the **composition of two** that are easy. Rotating an array with three reversals used the very same idea.
